prompt: You comb your hair on a dry day and it stands on end. What has actually moved?
options: Electrons, from your hair onto the comb
Protons, from the comb into your hair
Heat, from the comb into your hair
Air, pushed in between the hairs
correctAnswer: Electrons, from your hair onto the comb
explanation: Electrons leave your hair for the comb. The comb ends up negative and every hair positive, and like charges repel, so the hairs push apart.

prompt: Franklin's famous kite was struck by lightning, and the bolt charged his Leyden jar.
explanation: This is the myth. The Franklin Institute says the kite was not struck; if it had been, he would probably have been electrocuted. It picked up the charge already in the stormy air.

prompt: Current is measured in amps: one amp is one _____ of charge passing a point every second.
explanation: Current is the rate of charge flow, so one ampere is one coulomb of charge per second.

prompt: You wire a cell, a resistor, a switch and an LED in a loop and close the switch. Every joint is sound, but the LED stays dark. What do you try first?
options: Turn the LED round
Add a second switch
Wet the wires so they conduct better
Take the resistor out and touch the LED straight to a shop battery
explanation: An LED only lights one way round, so flipping it is the first fix. Wiring an LED straight to a shop battery is likely to wreck it.

prompt: Match each word to what it means in a circuit:

pairs.right: The push: energy per unit of charge
How hard the path fights back
Stores charge, then dumps it in one burst

explanation: Voltage pushes, current flows, resistance resists, and a Leyden jar releases all its stored energy in a single burst, unlike a true battery.

prompt: A storm is coming. You see a flash and count 15 seconds before the thunder. Roughly how far away was the strike?
options: About 3 miles (5 km)
About 15 miles (24 km)
About half a mile
Directly overhead
explanation: Thunder covers about a mile every 5 seconds, so 15 seconds is about 3 miles. And if you can hear thunder at all, you are already within striking distance: get indoors.

prompt: A friend explains how a thundercloud makes lightning. Which step is wrong?
steps: Collisions between ice and hail in the cloud separate electric charge.
Light ice crystals carry positive charge up to the top of the cloud.
The middle of the cloud becomes negatively charged.
Air is an excellent conductor, so charge leaks quietly to the ground all the time.
When the difference grows too great, the air breaks down in a giant spark.
explanation: Air is an insulator. That is why charge builds up at all, until the difference grows too great and the air breaks down in a flash.

prompt: Put these moments in the early story of electricity in order:
steps: Gilbert publishes De Magnete and gives us the word electricity
Von Kleist and Musschenbroek make the Leyden jar
Franklin flies his kite in a thunderstorm
Richmann is killed trying a similar experiment
explanation: De Magnete came out in 1600; the Leyden jar arrived around 1745; Franklin's kite flew in 1752; and Richmann died a year later.

prompt: You have a lemon and a pile of scrap. Which pair, pushed into the lemon, makes a working cell?
options: A copper strip and a galvanised nail
Two copper strips
Two galvanised nails
A copper strip and a plastic straw
correctAnswer: A copper strip and a galvanised nail
explanation: A cell needs two different metals and a liquid that carries ions. A galvanised nail is coated with zinc, and copper pulls electrons more strongly than zinc.

prompt: The energy in a lemon battery comes from the lemon juice itself.
explanation: This is the myth. The juice is only the wet layer that carries ions. The energy comes from the metals, above all the zinc, which is slowly eaten away.

prompt: One lemon gives less than 1 volt. To light an LED that needs about 2 volts, you join three or four lemons in _____, copper of one to zinc of the next.
explanation: Joined in series, copper to zinc, the lemons' voltages add up, exactly as the cells in Volta's pile do.

prompt: Your four-lemon chain reads nearly 3 volts on a meter, enough for the LED, yet the LED only just glows. What is the most likely reason?
options: Each lemon can push only a feeble current
The voltage is far too high and the LED is burning out
Lemon cells work only in sunlight
Copper blocks the current
correctAnswer: Each lemon can push only a feeble current
explanation: Stacking cells adds volts, but a weak cell still delivers only a feeble current. Even the BBC's Baghdad battery report pointed to current as the real limit.

prompt: Match each person to their part in the story of the battery:

pairs.right: A pile of metal discs and wet cloth

explanation: Galvani's frogs started the argument, Volta's pile settled it, and others quickly used the pile to split water and discover new elements.

prompt: Why did adding more zinc, wet cloth and copper sandwiches make Volta's pile stronger?
options: The voltages of the cells add up
More cloth soaks up more charge from the air
Each sandwich stores one separate spark
A heavier pile presses the metals together harder
correctAnswer: The voltages of the cells add up
explanation: Each sandwich is one cell, roughly 0.75 volts in Volta's first piles, and the voltages of cells stacked in series add together.

prompt: Someone argues that the Baghdad battery proves ancient electricity. Which step does not follow?
steps: The jar held a copper cylinder around an iron rod.
Replicas filled with vinegar or grape juice give 0.8 to nearly 2 volts.
So a jar like it could work as a cell.
Therefore it must have been used as a battery.
Yet no wires have been found, and similar jars from Seleucia are thought to have held scrolls.
explanation: Being able to work as a cell is not evidence of being used as one. With no wires and a plausible scroll-jar explanation, the leap in step 4 is the error.

prompt: Put the steps for building a lemon battery in order:
steps: Roll each lemon firmly to free the juice
Push a copper strip and a galvanised nail into each lemon
Wire the copper of one lemon to the zinc of the next
Connect the free zinc and copper ends to the LED
If it stays dark, turn the LED round
explanation: Free the juice, add two different metals, chain the cells so their voltages add, connect the load, and only then troubleshoot the LED's direction.

prompt: What made Ørsted's compass needle move in 1820?
options: Connecting or disconnecting a circuit near it
Heating it over a candle
Thunder rolling outside
Rubbing it with fur
correctAnswer: Connecting or disconnecting a circuit near it
explanation: Whenever Ørsted connected or disconnected his circuit to a voltaic pile, the nearby compass needle moved: the first clear sign that electricity and magnetism are linked.

prompt: There is good evidence that Faraday told a prime minister his discovery would one day be taxed.
explanation: This is the myth. The line appears in no account by Faraday or his contemporaries, and Gladstone did not become prime minister until the year after Faraday died.

prompt: Faraday found that a magnet held perfectly still inside a coil makes _____ current.
explanation: Only a change in the magnetic field through the coil induces a voltage. A magnet sitting still makes none.

prompt: You shake your tube generator hard. The magnets slide freely but the LED never flashes, even when you turn it round. What is the most likely fault?
options: The lacquer was not scraped off the wire ends
The magnets are moving too fast
The tube is made of clear plastic
The room is too dark
correctAnswer: The lacquer was not scraped off the wire ends
explanation: Magnet wire is coated in insulating lacquer. Unless you scrape it off the ends, the copper never touches the clips and no current can reach the LED.

prompt: Match each discovery to its maker:

pairs.left: A current swings a compass needle (1820)
A wire circles a magnet in mercury, the first motor
Current in one coil on an iron ring makes a brief current in the other
A theory of the effect, begun within a week of the news

explanation: Ørsted found the link, Ampère built the theory, and Faraday turned it into the motor and then, in 1831, into induction.

prompt: You are hand-cranking a dynamo when a friend switches its lamp on. What do you feel?
options: The handle suddenly gets harder to turn
The handle gets easier to turn
Nothing changes at all
The handle tries to spin backwards
correctAnswer: The handle suddenly gets harder to turn
explanation: Lenz's law: the induced current makes a magnetic field that opposes the motion. The moment the lamp draws current, the generator pushes back on your hand.

prompt: Here is an account of Faraday's iron ring experiment. Which step is wrong?
steps: Faraday wound two separate insulated coils on an iron ring.
He joined coil A to a battery and coil B to a meter.
When he connected the battery, the meter needle jumped.
While the current kept flowing, the needle stayed deflected to one side.
When he broke the circuit, the needle swung the other way.
explanation: Faraday wrote that though the contact was continued, the effect was not permanent: the needle soon came back to rest. Only changes in the current induce a current.

prompt: Put the steps for building the shake generator in order:
steps: Roll plastic sheets into a tube
Wind about 500 turns of magnet wire round the middle
Scrape the lacquer off the wire ends
Clip the bare ends to an LED
Load the magnet stack and cap the tube
Shake hard and watch for flashes
explanation: Tube, coil, bare ends, LED, magnets, then shake: each pass of the magnets through the coil induces a pulse of current.

prompt: An old 40-watt bulb runs for five hours. How much energy has it used?
options: 200 watt-hours
45 watt-hours
8 watt-hours
40 watt-hours
explanation: Energy is power multiplied by time: 40 watts for 5 hours is 200 watt-hours, or 0.2 kilowatt-hours.

prompt: Solar panels produce nothing at all on a cloudy day.
explanation: This is the myth. Flat panels can use scattered (diffuse) light as well as the direct beam, so they keep working under cloud, just at lower output.

prompt: Natural Resources Canada estimates a stream's power in kilowatts as flow × _____ × 9.8 × efficiency.
explanation: Head is the height the water falls. Flow in cubic metres a second times head in metres times gravity times an efficiency of 0.5 to 0.7 gives kilowatts.

prompt: Stream A falls 10 metres with 0.3 cubic metres of water a second. Stream B falls 2 metres with 10 litres a second. Roughly what can each give?
options: A about 15 kW, B about 100 W
Both about 15 kW
A about 100 W, B about 15 kW
Both about 100 W
correctAnswer: A about 15 kW, B about 100 W
explanation: A: 0.3 × 10 × 9.8 × 0.5 is about 15 kW. B: 0.01 × 2 × 9.8 × 0.5 is about 0.1 kW. Head and flow make all the difference.

prompt: Match each power source to the fact that goes with it:

pairs.right: Grinding grain for more than 2,000 years
Wants an average wind of at least 4 m/s

explanation: Each source has its own character: ancient water wheels, round-the-clock micro-hydro, wind that needs a good site, and solar cells that must be chained into panels.

prompt: A small home wind turbine is rated at 10 kW. Why might it give far less most of the time?
options: It reaches its rating only in a strong wind
Wind turbines work only at night
Longer blades produce less power
The rating is for each blade separately
correctAnswer: It reaches its rating only in a strong wind
explanation: A rating is the most the machine can deliver. In lighter winds it gives much less, which is why wind and solar systems need storage.

prompt: A survivor sizes a hydro scheme. Which step is wrong?
steps: The stream carries 0.01 cubic metres of water a second.
It falls 2 metres to the wheel.
That comes to about 10 kW, plenty to run a whole house.
So they will still need batteries and frugal LED lights.
explanation: 0.01 × 2 × 9.8 × 0.5 is about 0.1 kW, a hundred watts, not 10 kW. A garden stream lights a few LEDs, not a whole house.

prompt: An elite 70 kg cyclist can hold 350 watts for an hour. Ignoring losses, how long must they pedal to supply the 200 watt-hours a 40-watt bulb uses in five hours?
options: About 35 minutes
About 5 hours
About 6 minutes
About 2 hours
explanation: 200 watt-hours divided by 350 watts is about 0.57 hours, roughly 35 minutes of elite effort, which is why LEDs and real power sources matter.

prompt: Which kind of battery did Gaston Planté invent in 1859, the first that could be recharged?
options: Lead-acid
Lithium-ion
Lemon cell
Voltaic pile
explanation: Planté's lead-acid battery was the first rechargeable battery, and its descendants sit in almost every car on the road.

prompt: Rubber-soled shoes will keep you safe if you touch mains wiring.
explanation: This is the myth. Insulation must be suitable for the voltage and conditions, moisture can make insulators conduct, and shoes do nothing if your body joins both wires of a circuit.

prompt: The HSE warns that normal mains voltage, _____ volts AC in Britain, can kill.
explanation: Mains at 230 volts can drive a lethal current through a body. That is why every build in this skill stays at battery voltage.

prompt: You find someone slumped against a faulty heater, still touching it. What do you do?
options: Do not touch them; turn off the electricity at the source
Grab their arm and pull them clear
Throw a bucket of water over them
Start chest compressions straight away while they are touching it
correctAnswer: Do not touch them; turn off the electricity at the source
explanation: St John Ambulance: do not touch a casualty still in contact with the source, or you risk electrocution yourself. Break the contact first, then call 999 or 112 and treat them.

prompt: Match each current, flowing hand to foot for one second, to its effect:

pairs.right: Breathing can stop; death is possible

explanation: It takes remarkably little current to kill: a tenth of an amp is in the deadly range, which is why mains voltage is so dangerous.

prompt: You are wiring LED camp lights to a 12-volt battery. Where should the fuse go?
options: First in line from the battery's positive terminal
At the far end, after the last lamp
Nowhere: fuses just waste power
Directly across the two battery terminals
correctAnswer: First in line from the battery's positive terminal
explanation: A fuse melts when too much current flows and protects the wire after it from overheating, so it must come first. A fuse across the terminals would simply be a short circuit.

prompt: A friend reasons about working on a car battery. Which step is wrong?
steps: A car battery is only 12 volts.
Twelve volts cannot push much current through dry skin, so the shock risk is low.
So a car battery is completely safe to work on.
A spanner dropped across its terminals carries a huge current and gets very hot very quickly.
Charging it also makes hydrogen, which a spark can ignite.
explanation: Low voltage does not mean low hazard. Short circuits can burn you and charging gases can explode, which is why the HSE asks for goggles, insulated tools and no metal jewellery.

prompt: A hiker is struck by lightning and collapses. A bystander is afraid to touch her. What is true?
options: The body does not store electricity, so it is safe to touch her and give first aid
She stays electrified for several minutes
Only someone in rubber gloves may touch her
Touching her will draw another strike
correctAnswer: The body does not store electricity, so it is safe to touch her and give first aid
explanation: The National Weather Service is clear: the human body does not store electricity, and believing otherwise could cost a life. Someone still touching a live wire is a different case.
